title: Flashcards
dek: Short definitions of concepts used in real work. Cards are added only after a concept comes up in practice.

categories.title: Python
categories.blurb: Core syntax, data structures, errors, files, packages and the web.

cards.def: An ordered collection of items in square brackets. Items can be changed after creation.
Reading one item by its position. Positions start at 0. A negative index counts from the end.
Replace the item at a position with `list[i] = value`.
Returns how many items a list holds, or how many characters a string holds.
A list whose items are lists. The first index picks the inner list, the second picks the item inside it.
cards.code:
t = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
t[1][2]    # 6  (list 1, item 2)
len(t)     # 2  (number of inner lists)
len(t[0])  # 3  (items in the first inner list)

cards.def: `seq[start:stop]` returns a new sequence from start up to, but not including, stop. A missing start means the beginning; a missing stop means the end.
`seq[::-1]` returns a reversed copy. The original is unchanged.
Gives the items from last to first so a loop can walk backwards. It does not change the original.
`[x] * n` builds a list holding x n times. For a mutable item such as a list, every slot holds the SAME object.
Two names (or two slots) referring to the same object, so a change through one shows up through the other. Build independent inner lists with a comprehension, not with repetition.
cards.code:
bad  = [[0] * 3] * 2                 # one row, shown twice
good = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(2)]   # two separate rows
bad[0][0] = 9    # bad is now [[9,0,0],[9,0,0]]

cards.def: A loop written inside brackets that builds a new list: `[expression for name in sequence]`. Add `if condition` at the end to keep only some items.
Produces the integers 0 up to n-1. `range(a, b)` runs from a up to b-1. Used to repeat something a set number of times.
Return the largest and smallest item. Both raise ValueError on an empty sequence.
Adds the items. True counts as 1 and False as 0, so summing comparisons counts how many are true.
An empty list, string or tuple counts as False in a condition. Use `if not items:` to guard against empty input.
`x in seq` is True when x is one of the items of a list, or a substring of a string.
Indexes start at 0, so the count of positions is the largest index plus one.
A fixed group of values in parentheses. Index it like a list, but it cannot be changed after creation.
Naming every piece of a tuple (or list) in one statement. The number of names must match the number of items.
Put several names in the loop header to unpack each item as you go.
cards.code:
for name, age in [("Rex", 3), ("Tom", 5)]:
    print(name, age)

cards.def: Runs the indented block once for each item of a sequence, one item at a time.
A loop inside a loop. The inner loop finishes completely for every turn of the outer loop. Use it to visit every cell of a 2D list.
Start a variable at 0, then add to it inside a loop whenever a condition holds.
Adds to a variable in place. `x += 1` means `x = x + 1`.
`=` assigns a value to a name. `==` compares two values and gives True or False.
A `return` inside an `if` lets a function exit before the rest of its body, which handles special cases first.
Defines a function: a name, parameters in parentheses, and an indented body. The body runs only when the function is called.
Sends a value back to whoever called the function, then ends the function. A return does not pass through a second function on its own.
A function with no `return` statement gives back None. Calling a function without using or returning its result throws the value away.
Python's value for "nothing". Often returned to signal that there is no result.
A statement that does nothing. It holds an empty function or block in place until you fill it in.
Splitting a job into small functions, each with one input type and one output type, so each can be tested alone.
cards.code:
def read(path): ...
def parse(text): ...
def report(rows): ...

cards.def: A string placed first in a function that states what it takes, returns and does. Shown by help().
Code under this line runs only when the file is run directly, not when it is imported by another file.
Shows text in the terminal and ends the line. It returns None; it does not hand back a value.
`sep.join(list_of_strings)` returns one string with sep placed between the items. Every item must already be a string.
Converts a value to a string. Needed before joining or gluing numbers into text.
A string starting with `f` where `{name}` is replaced by the value of an expression.
Returns how many times sub appears in the string.
Returns the index of the first match, or -1 if sub is not found.
Returns a new string with every old replaced by new. The original is unchanged.
Returns the string without whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines) at both ends.
True when x is a value of the given type.
Runs the try block line by line. If a line raises a matching error, Python skips the rest of try and jumps to except. With no error, except is skipped.
A `return` in a try block runs only if Python reaches it. If an earlier line raises, control jumps to except and that return never happens.
Name the error type in `except`. A bare `except:` hides unrelated mistakes such as typos.
Errors form families. Catching a parent class also catches all its children.
A function that does no try/except passes its error up to its caller. Use this when the caller should decide what to do.
Signals an error on purpose and stops the current function.
cards.code:
if n < 0:
    raise ValueError("n must be >= 0")

cards.def: Read the last line first: it names the error type and message. The lines above show the file and line number where it happened.
cards.code:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "app.py", line 3, in <module>
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

cards.def: An operation got a value of the wrong type, such as indexing a list with a string or joining numbers.
The type is right but the value is not acceptable, such as max of an empty list.
The import names a package that is not installed in the Python that is running the file.
Print a value after each step and compare it to what you expect. The first step where they differ points to the bug.
Opens a file. Mode "r" reads, "w" writes and replaces the contents, "a" appends.
Opens a file and closes it automatically when the indented block ends, even after an error.
cards.code:
with open("notes.txt") as f:
    text = f.read()

cards.def: read returns the whole file as one string. write puts text into a file opened for writing.
cards.code:
with open("a.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("hello\n")

cards.def: Tells open how text is stored. Set it explicitly so symbols and non-English characters survive, especially on Windows.
Loads a module or package so its names can be used in your file.
Downloads a third-party package into a specific Python. Use `python -m pip install name` so pip belongs to the same Python as `python`.
A computer can have several Python installs, each with its own packages. A package installed into one is invisible to the others.
The path of the Python that is running your code. Print it to see which install you are using.
From a terminal, `python file.py` runs a file with the Python found first on PATH. An editor's run button may use a different interpreter.
Ctrl+Shift+P, then "Python: Select Interpreter", sets which Python the editor uses for the run button.
The client sends a request; the server sends back a response. A script that downloads a page is a client.
The address of a resource. Parts: scheme (https), host (example.com), path (/a/b), optional query (?q=1).
The request method that means "give me this resource". It should not change anything on the server.
A number in the response that says what happened. 2xx succeeded, 3xx redirected, 4xx a problem with the request, 5xx a server problem.
The text a web page is written in. Content sits inside tags such as table, tr, td, p and a.
Sends a GET request and returns a Response. It does not raise for 404 or 500. Always set timeout in seconds, or a stuck server freezes the program.
`.status_code` is the integer code, `.text` is the body as a string, `.headers` holds extra information such as Content-Type.
cards.code:
r.status_code   # 200
r.text          # the page body
r.headers["Content-Type"]

cards.def: Does nothing for 2xx responses. Raises requests.HTTPError for 4xx and 5xx. Call it right after the request.
The parent of every error requests raises (HTTPError, ConnectionError, Timeout, bad URL). Catch it to handle all network failures in one place.
A script is logged out. A page that needs sign-in returns a login page, not the data. Check the status code and look for expected content.
Save fetched HTML to a file or print a slice of it, so you can see its structure before writing code to read it.
